title: The Skates of Wrath
bodyHtml:
Here are some words in Sauk1 and their unmatched English translations in alphabetical order.

1. âchimowaA. computer
2. anemôhaB. dog
3. anemôhêhaC. Ferris wheel
4. chîtapikânekiD. foal2
5. chîtapiwaE. laundromat
6. kôkenikânekiF. library
7. mehikowîthenikânekiG. living room
8. meshitêtêpithoniH. metal
9. meshotênekiI. Mexican restaurant
10. methenahikanani âchimôniJ. newspaper
11. methenahikaniK. oats / hay
12. methenahikanikânekiL. Oklahoma City2
13. pîwâpehkwiM. paper
14. pîwâpehkwi âchimôniN. puppy
15. pîwâpehkwi wînêtepiO. roller skates
16. têtêpithonani mahkathêhaniP. telephone
17. tôskashi wîtheniweniQ. to sit
18. tôskashêhâR. to tell

G1. Determine the correct correspondences.

G2. Translate the following into English: tôskashâ, kôkenêwa

G3. Translate the following into Sauk: brain, shoe store, town

1 Sauk is an Algonquian language spoken in Iowa, Kansas, and Oklahoma. Like many Indigenous languages of North America, Sauk was negatively impacted by European colonization and is now at risk of extinction. Today, Sauk is spoken by several hundred people; of these people, only a handful speak Sauk monolingually (i.e., as their only language). However, recent revitalization efforts, including courses on Sauk offered in schools, may help slow or reverse its decline.

2 A foal is a young horse. Oklahoma City is Oklahoma's capital and largest city.

questions.partPrompt: Determine the correct correspondences. For each Sauk word, write the letter of its English translation.

hints.text: Do not start from the English. First sort the eighteen Sauk items into families that share a beginning: the two anemôh- words, the two chîtapi- words, the three methenahikan- words, the three pîwâpehkwi words, the two tôskash- words. Within a family the English meanings must be related too.

Sauk builds long words out of pieces. Look for one recurring ending that turns a word into the name of a place, another that means "little" or "young", one that marks the "to X" form of a verb, and one that marks plurals. Some items are two words side by side, which means a compound: a word for a material or an animal plus a second word. Match the English glosses that are themselves transparent compounds (a place where something happens, a young animal, a thing made of metal) to the Sauk items with the matching shape.

Here is the kind of step you need, done on structure rather than on any of the answers. Items 13, 14 and 15 all begin with the same free-standing word pîwâpehkwi, so 14 and 15 must each be that word compounded with something else, and whatever pîwâpehkwi means alone will show up inside both English glosses. Notice also that item 16 has the same ending -ani appearing twice, an ending you can see again in item 10, so item 16 is two nouns that are both marked the same way. Sorting the items by shape like this narrows the English candidates before you commit to any single pairing.

explanationHtml:
The plan: shapes first, meanings second

With eighteen words and eighteen glosses there are far too many possible matchings to guess. The way in is to notice that Sauk words are built out of smaller pieces (morphemes), and that several of the English glosses are also built out of pieces we can see: a puppy is a young dog, a foal is a young horse, a laundromat is a place where you wash, a living room is a place where you sit. So group the Sauk items by their shared parts, group the English items by their shared parts, and line the two groupings up.

Families of Sauk words

Sorting the list by shared beginnings gives:

  • anemôha / anemôhêha
  • chîtapiwa / chîtapikâneki
  • kôkenikâneki, mehikowîthenikâneki
  • methenahikani / methenahikanikâneki / methenahikanani âchimôni
  • pîwâpehkwi / pîwâpehkwi âchimôni / pîwâpehkwi wînêtepi
  • tôskashi wîtheniweni / tôskashêhâ
  • meshitêtêpithoni / meshotêneki (both begin mesh-)
  • âchimowa, chîtapiwa (both end -wa)
  • têtêpithonani mahkathêhani

The recurring pieces

-kâneki = "place" (a locative ending). Four items end in it: a place for sitting is a living room, a place for washing is a laundromat, a place for paper is a library, and a place for Mexican food is a Mexican restaurant. That single ending pins down four glosses at once.

-êha / -êhâ = "little, young" (a diminutive ending). anemôha plus this ending is the young version of whatever anemôha is, and tôskash- plus this ending is the young version of whatever tôskash- is. The English list contains exactly two young-animal words, puppy and foal, and footnote 2 tells you a foal is a young horse. So the anemôh- pair must be the dog pair and the tôskash- pair must be the horse pair.

-wa = the "to X" form of a verb (an infinitive). Only two glosses are verbs, to sit and to tell. chîtapiwa is the verb whose place-form is the living room, so it is to sit, and âchimowa is to tell.

-ani = plural. Compare methenahikani with methenahikanani: the second is the plural of the first. In têtêpithonani mahkathêhani both nouns carry that plural marking, which fits roller skates (wheels plus shoes, both plural).

mesh- = "big". meshitêtêpithoni contains têtêpithon- "wheel" (seen again in the skates item), so a big wheel is the Ferris wheel. meshotêneki is then "big town", which the footnote helps you read as Oklahoma City, the state's largest city.

Compounds with âchimôni

âchimôni is built on the same root as to tell, so it means something like "telling, message". A telling made of paper is a newspaper; a telling made of metal is a telephone. That means methenahikani is paper and pîwâpehkwi is metal. The remaining pîwâpehkwi compound, with wînêtepi, is the computer - a "metal brain" - so wînêtepi on its own means brain, which answers part of G3.

Finishing the leftovers

tôskashi wîtheniweni is "horse food", which matches oats / hay. That confirms tôskash- is the horse root, and the leftover animal item anemôha is dog with anemôhêha its puppy.

G2: reading new words

tôskashâ is the horse root with no diminutive ending, so it is simply horse. kôkenêwa has the infinitive -wa on the root found in the laundromat word, so it is to wash.

G3: building new words

brain is wînêtepi, extracted from the computer compound. For shoe store, take the shoe word from the skates item and add the place ending: mahkathêhanikâneki (shoe-PL-LOC); the solution also accepts mahkathêhikâneki (shoe-LOC) if you strip the plural first. For town, remove "big" from meshotêneki to get otêneki; because the boundary between mesh- and the town word can be cut in more than one sensible place, the official key also accepts têneki, otênekéhi, tênekéhi, otênehéki and tênehéki.

The moral

Matching puzzles like this are really morphology puzzles: find the affixes and the compounds, and the meanings sort themselves out. Almost every match here was forced by a piece of structure rather than guessed from meaning.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys taken from the official solution page. G1 keys are the option letters (solution prints e.g. "1. R (tell-INF)"); the parenthetical morpheme glosses were not included in the keys. Points distributed as G1 0.5 each (9), G2 1.5 each (3), G3 1 each (3) = 15; the official solution shows no per-part breakdown, so please confirm. G1 choices are given as bare letters A-R so the key matches character-for-character; the booklet prints them as "A. computer" etc. The booklet prints no fill-in blanks (answers go on separate answer sheets), so no answer slots were embedded in bodyHtml. Check all circumflex/acute diacritics in Sauk data, especially otênekéhi / tênekéhi / otênehéki / tênehéki in the G3 accepted variants.
